subtype: Approach: promising things outside the role's power [Pitfall]
passage: The assembly hall was hot, the microphone squealed, and each candidate had ninety seconds. Mehak looked at the restless rows and decided ordinary promises would not be heard. "If I'm captain: no homework on Fridays! And free trips to the water park every term!" The hall roared. She grinned, dizzy with it. Behind the stage, Bhupen Sir, the civics teacher, frowned. "A captain can't cancel homework or approve trips, Mehak. Those aren't yours to promise." By the next day, students who had cheered were saying, "She can't do that." A Class 10 student told her, "I'd rather vote for someone who tells the truth." Mehak's stomach turned. She had won the applause and lost something she had not known she needed.

qa.q: How long did each candidate have to speak?
How did Mehak feel after the applause, and how did it change?
qa.a: Mehak felt dizzy and pleased at first, but her stomach turned once students began doubting her and a Class 10 student asked for honesty.

qa.q: What could Mehak have promised instead, and why?
qa.a: Mehak could have promised things a captain can do, such as asking staff about a sports-day slot and setting up a suggestion box, because those can be delivered and keep trust.

qa.q: How does Bhupen Sir see the promises?
qa.a: Bhupen Sir sees claims that cannot be delivered, which would harm Mehak's credibility with teachers and with students who value honesty.

grounding: The candidate promises no homework and free trips, and the claims win applause but cannot be delivered, harming credibility with teachers and with students who value honesty.

passage:
The Class 11 election assembly in the Lajpat Nagar school hall was noisy even before Rashmi stood up.

"If I'm school captain," she shouted, "no homework on weekends! And two free trips every year!"

The hall roared. Her friends banged the benches. Nikita, standing at the back, didn't clap.

Afterwards, the maths teacher stopped Rashmi in the corridor. "Who is going to cancel homework? You?" Rashmi laughed it off, but her cheeks went red.

The next week, a Class 12 boy asked her at the canteen, "So when's the first free trip?" Rashmi mumbled something about "talking to management". He shook his head and walked away.

She won by a small margin. By the end of the term, whenever she promised anything, even something small like a suggestion box, people just said, "Sure, like the trips."

qa.q: What two things did Rashmi promise in her speech?
qa.a: She promised no homework on weekends and two free trips every year.

qa.q: What do Rashmi's red cheeks suggest when the maths teacher questions her?
qa.a: They suggest she felt embarrassed and caught out, knowing the promise was not in her power, even while she laughed it off.

qa.q: Which kind of promise would have served Rashmi better, and why?
qa.a: Small promises she could really deliver, like the suggestion box, would have built trust; bold ones won applause but made later promises sound empty.

qa.q: How might Nikita, who did not clap, have seen the speech?
qa.a: Nikita probably felt sceptical and uneasy, noticing the promises sounded good but could not be kept by a student captain.

grounding: Shows a candidate promising no homework and free trips, winning applause but losing credibility with teachers and students because the claims cannot be delivered.

subtype: Approach: promising things outside the role's power [Pitfall]
passage:
"Devika, you can't promise a swimming pool," Gurleen said, reading the poster draft in the art room.

"Why not? Everyone wants one."

"Because the school doesn't have land for it, and you're a student. What happens in March when there's no pool?"

"People will forget."

"They won't. Remember Harsh last year? 'Canteen will be free.' They still call him Free Canteen."

Devika stuck the poster up anyway. At the assembly the cheer was huge. She grinned at Gurleen.

Two weeks after she won, the principal called her in. "Parents are asking about the pool." Devika stood in the office, silent.

In the corridor later she said quietly, "I can't even get the water cooler fixed now. Nobody believes me."

Gurleen sighed. "Start with the cooler. Then keep your word."

qa.q: What did Devika promise on her poster?
How did Devika feel when she said nobody believed her anymore?
qa.a: Devika felt discouraged and ashamed, realising the empty promise had cost her trust even for small, real fixes.

qa.q: What would you change first in Devika's campaign?
qa.a: Replace the pool with one promise she can control, like pushing for the cooler repair, so the applause she wins is backed by delivery.

qa.q: How might the principal have felt when parents asked about the pool?
qa.a: The principal was probably annoyed and put in an awkward spot, having to answer for a promise the school never made.

grounding: Shows a candidate winning cheers with a promise beyond a student's power, then losing credibility when it cannot be delivered.
